title: NEB Class 11 Physics — Vectors — 2020
subject: physics
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Differentiate between scalar and vector quantities with examples.
questions.solution:
**Scalar quantity:** A physical quantity that has **magnitude only** and obeys the ordinary rules of algebra.
- Has **no direction**.
- Added by simple arithmetic.
- Examples: mass, time, temperature, distance, speed, work, energy, electric charge, volume.

**Vector quantity:** A physical quantity that has **both magnitude and direction** and obeys the law of vector (triangle or parallelogram) addition.
- Changes with direction.
- Cannot be added by simple arithmetic; its component form is $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$.
- Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, electric field, weight.

**Note:** Speed is the scalar counterpart of velocity, and mass is the scalar counterpart of weight.
questions.knowledgeNote: Scalars have magnitude only and add arithmetically; vectors have magnitude and direction and follow vector addition.
questions.answer: **Scalar:** a quantity fully specified by **magnitude (and unit) alone** — no direction; scalars add by ordinary arithmetic. *Examples:* mass (5 kg), time, temperature, speed, distance, energy, work, density, electric charge. **Vector:** a quantity specified by **magnitude and direction**, obeying **vector (triangle/parallelogram) addition** — direction matters and vectors add head-to-tail. *Examples:* displacement (5 m east), velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, torque, electric field. **Key differences:** (1) direction — a vector needs it, a scalar doesn't; (2) addition — arithmetic vs geometric (two 5 N forces can give anything from 0 to 10 N); (3) multiplication — scalars multiply normally, vectors multiply via dot (scalar result) or cross (vector result) products. **Deep point:** speed vs velocity is the minimal pair — same magnitude, but only one carries a direction; whether a quantity needs a direction is a physical fact, not a convention.
